description: A very tight project schedule forced the usability consultants to compress user research, design and iteration into an eight-week period and work at top speed with only two consultants.
justification: The severe time constraint limited the team's ability to run planned iterations, thorough interviews, and evaluation cycles, hindering integration of feedback & iteration and evaluation workloads.
reference_excerpt: The project group had worked for five months nailing down the organizational requirements and their time was running out. ... Therefore the UCD process could not take more than eight weeks. ... it was judged that we would be able to deliver on time by working with two consultants on top speed.

description: PPG members were restricted in hands-on participation (only one member allowed to attend each interview or exercise) and consultants worked off-site, limiting stakeholder engagement.
justification: These constraints reduced meaningful stakeholder involvement and shared first-hand insight, impeding manage user understanding, facilitate user involvement, and coordination between designers and procurers.
reference_excerpt: In order to not interfere too much with the actual interviews only one member of the PPG was allowed to attend on each interview session. ... they comment that they should have participated more in the activities and that all work should have been done in their offices, instead of having the usability consultants work in their own office.

description: The project's organizational requirements were abstract, contradictory, and not specified to the same level as the user requirements, and the PPG failed to detail them when asked.
justification: Because organizational requirements were not sufficiently concretized by the procuring stakeholders, designers could not reliably align or justify design decisions, hindering specification of requirements and integration of user and business perspectives.
reference_excerpt: We identified the organizational requirements first and they did not reach the same level of concretization as the users’ requirements. ... The PPG had not been able to detail these to the level that the user requirements were specified.

description: A perceived power imbalance emerged because the usability company led the process strongly with their methodology, which made PPG members feel that the consultants had become 'too strong'.
justification: This trust and power dynamic caused the PPG to lose confidence in participating and ultimately halt the project, disrupting iteration and coordination across the multidisciplinary team and stopping planned design progress.
reference_excerpt: …but then… the usability company got to strong somehow. The usability company was much more professional in some way – they had their methodology and they knew where to go and so forth. But we, who sat with the organizational requirements, ... we were not as good at steering, so to speak.

description: Planned user evaluation activities were curtailed: only one of two planned card-sorting exercises was performed and some user categories were omitted from the respondent selection.
justification: Limiting or missing planned user studies reduced the designers' ability to fully understand segmentation and validate the information architecture, hindering understanding context of use and evaluation of designs.
reference_excerpt: Card-sorting exercises were planned with the two most important user groups, but only one could be performed. ... When the personas were discussed the PPG noticed that two categories of users seemed to be missing. The selection of respondents had not included these user groups.

justification: Low design literacy among stakeholders increased the need for designers to spend time on explanation rather than advancing design decisions, hindering coordination of the multidisciplinary team and efficient integration of feedback.
reference_excerpt: Since the members had varying experiences of working with design the discussion was not always smooth and concepts such as navigation levels had got to be explained.

description: Intercontinental and intercultural communication, plus language differences, complicated engagement with on-site user groups and required interpreters.
justification: These knowledge and language gaps impeded managing deep user understanding and facilitating participatory evaluations because translators and remote communication reduced direct access to users' native-language expressions and nuance.
reference_excerpt: The particular challenge in this project is the intercontinental and intercultural communication with the user groups on-site since the development team consists of German physicians and computer scientists. Interviews were conducted in English, French, and Malagasy. Interpreters translated from French to English or Malagasy to English when necessary.

description: Socio-cultural hierarchies and norms caused some participant groups to withhold honest expression in certain settings, undermining participatory methods.
justification: Power dynamics and cultural norms limited authentic user feedback and participation, hindering the designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to capture accurate mental models for design decisions.
reference_excerpt: we first had to learn, with the help of resident physicians, that certain interview settings did not produce the needed outcome because, due to socio-cultural differences, certain groups of people did not express themselves freely or at all in some settings, which is a major problem for participatory design methods. Due to the cross-cultural characteristics of the region, a deliberate attempt for specific user groups was made to reduce the number of participants and homogenize by gender; otherwise, some of the evaluation participants may not express themselves honestly or at all.

justification: This external constraint limited designers' ability to adapt language for target users, hindering management of user understanding and reducing effectiveness of participatory evaluation feedback related to documentation.
reference_excerpt: Unfortunately, the revision of the manual, based on AI guidelines for medical devices, did not reduce the number of technical terms used, so all users commented negatively on this.

description: The usability evaluation had a low sample size and a participant pool heavily skewed toward people with prior healthcare work experience, limiting the representativeness of user input.
justification: These participant-sampling constraints directly hindered designers' ability to manage and deepen user understanding, facilitate broad user involvement, and robustly evaluate designs across diverse user groups.
reference_excerpt: Aside from a low sample size, the main limitation of the user testing portion of our evaluation is the lack of a homologous “stimuli” to test with participants. An additional limitation that may affect the generalizability of the results of this study is the large percentage (71 percent) of patients who had history of working in health care prior to participating in this study.

description: The team used a semi-structured design process without a strict schedule for testing and making improvements, which increased production speed but reduced experimental rigor.
justification: This methodological choice constrained the designers' ability to conduct rigorous, controlled evaluations and to systematically integrate feedback and iteration, reducing the reliability of design evaluation activities.
reference_excerpt: In the current study, we chose to implement a semi-structured design process that refrained from using a strict schedule to determine when to begin testing and making interface improvements during the design of the interface. This methodology increased the speed at which the interface could be produced at the cost of rigorous experimental design.

description: After equalizing visual ranges for different biomarkers, the designers created non-linear scales but did not assess how those non-linear representations affected patient perceptions.
justification: Failing to evaluate the impact of non-linear scales prevented designers from fully evaluating the holistic user experience and understanding potential unintended consequences of visual design changes.
reference_excerpt: An unanticipated consequence of this design adjustment was the creation of non-linear scales, where the visual space for each biomarker are radically different than the other. We did not make any attempt to assess the impact of these non-linear scales on patient perceptions.

description: Recruitment required participants to have internet access, a desktop or laptop with camera/microphone, and the usability protocol required use of Zoom, biasing the sample toward higher technological literacy.
justification: These participation requirements limited who could take part and therefore constrained the designers' ability to engage a representative range of users and to manage a comprehensive understanding of the target population, hindering Manage user understanding, Facilitate user involvement, and Understand context of use.
reference_excerpt:
Inclusion criteria for the workshop participants were as follows: they must (1) be aged ≥50 years; (2) have sustained at least one skeletal fracture after the age of 40 years; (3) be able to communicate in English; and (4) have access to the internet and own a desktop computer or laptop computer with a camera and microphone.

Third, the protocol for the usability tests required participants to have access to Zoom. Consequently, these participants likely had higher technological literacy than those who would never have used videoconferencing tools.

description: Convenience sampling (recruiting prior study participants and clinic patients) likely biased the participant pool toward individuals already familiar with osteoporosis and injury management.
justification: This sampling bias limited designers' ability to elicit broad, representative user requirements and to fully manage user understanding and specify requirements for less-informed users, hindering Manage user understanding and Specify user requirements workloads.
reference_excerpt: Second, convenience sampling may have biased our results, as we recruited participants who had participated in previous studies on bone health or who had been evaluated in orthopedic clinics at our center. Design workshop participants were well aware of osteoporosis and its negative impacts and may have had prior knowledge related to injury management.
